references_named: Frank Stella, "What you see is what you see" (1966 interview with Bruce Glaser)
rationale: The mechanism genuinely enacts Stella's deductive position: bands are computed from the live viewport edge with no stored image, so the picture is literally its frame thinking out loud. Double-coding lands cleanly — surface gag (a hard-edge monochrome) and literate argument (Stella's anti-illusionism, the readymade of a position). It sits firmly on the order end of the chance/order axis and answers the catalogue's existing viewport-driven works (Measurement: Viewport, The Responsive Eye) from the opposite direction: device conscripted to abolish illusion rather than produce it. Craft is restrained and complete; license and ethics are stated on-page.
reservations: Novelty is moderate: the viewport-as-stretcher move is already present in the catalogue (Measurement: Viewport, Hierarchy of Genres, Composition in Red, Yellow and Blue (32 × 32)), so the only-on-the-web claim is thinner than for stronger entries. The wit is dry but a touch flat — the joke that 'there is no image to be honest about' is the same joke the Stella quote already makes, and the work doesn't add a second layer of surprise (e.g., a console attestation, a refusal of some browser behavior, or a deliberate failure mode).
revision_suggestion: Add a single web-native gesture that the Stella quote cannot say on its own — for example, a console.log of the deduced band count and viewport, or a deliberate refusal (no right-click save, no canvas.toDataURL, or a print stylesheet that erases the bands) — so the work does something only the browser can do, not just render what a Stella canvas already does.
